claims.source: Severe forms of this disorder are accompanied by neurodevelopmental abnormalities including type II lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, brainstem and hindbrain hypoplasia, ocular dysplasia, and white matter defects (Godfrey et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Clinical features of dystroglycanopathy established in previous literature.

claims.claim: Glycosylated Dystroglycan regulates axon guidance in the developing spinal cord by maintaining the basement membrane as a permissive growth substrate.
claims.source: We previously found that glycosylated Dystroglycan regulates axon guidance in the developing spinal cord and in the optic chiasm by maintaining the basement membrane as a permissive growth substrate and organizing the extracellular localization of Slit proteins in the floor plate (Clements and Wright, 2018; Wright et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Glycosylated Dystroglycan regulates axon guidance by organizing the extracellular localization of Slit proteins in the floor plate.
claims.source: We previously found that glycosylated Dystroglycan regulates axon guidance in the developing spinal cord and in the optic chiasm by maintaining the basement membrane as a permissive growth substrate and organizing the extracellular localization of Slit proteins in the floor plate (Clements and Wright, 2018; Wright et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan protein is expressed in spinal commissural axons at E12.5.
claims.source: Examination of E12.5 spinal cord sections shows that in addition to its enrichment in the floor plate and the basement membrane (Figure 1A inset, arrows), Dystroglycan protein was detected in spinal commissural axons (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is enriched in the floor plate and basement membrane of the spinal cord at E12.5.
claims.source: Examination of E12.5 spinal cord sections shows that in addition to its enrichment in the floor plate and the basement membrane (Figure 1A inset, arrows), Dystroglycan protein was detected in spinal commissural axons (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In cultured E12.5 commissural axons, Dystroglycan is expressed throughout the axon, including the growth cone.
claims.source: In cultured e12.5 commissural axons, Dystroglycan was expressed throughout the axon, including the growth cone (arrows, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining of cultured neurons shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: All abnormal injection sites in Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants exhibit both stalling within the floorplate and anterior-posterior randomization of post-crossing axonal trajectory.
claims.source: This phenotype is fully penetrant, and all of the abnormal injections sites in Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants exhibited both stalling within the floorplate and an anterior-posterior (AP) randomization of post-crossing axonal trajectory.
claims.evidence: Observed in DiI labeling experiments and quantified in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: Post-crossing commissural axons in Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants exhibit abnormal bundling and disruptions along the ventrolateral funiculus.
claims.source: As we have previously shown, post-crossing commissural axons in Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants exhibit abnormal bundling and disruptions along the ventrolateral funiculus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1, Robo1, and Robo2 antibody staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The ventrolateral funiculus appears normal in both Dag1βcyto/- and Dag1F/-;Wnt1Cre mutants.
claims.source: In contrast, he ventrolateral funiculus appears normal in both Dag1βcyto/- and Dag1F/-;Wnt1Cre mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F), confirming the results obtained with open book preparations.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1, Robo1, and Robo2 antibody staining shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is expressed by neuroepithelial cells at E14.5.
claims.source: At E14.5, Dystroglycan is expressed by neuroepithelial cells and is enriched in the basement membrane surrounding the brain.
claims.evidence: Observed by immunostaining as described in the text.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is enriched in the basement membrane surrounding the brain at E14.5.
claims.source: At E14.5, Dystroglycan is expressed by neuroepithelial cells and is enriched in the basement membrane surrounding the brain.
claims.evidence: Observed by immunostaining as described in the text.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is present in the ventral telencephalon, particularly in axons in the thalamus and the developing internal capsule at E14.5.
claims.source: It is also present in the ventral telencephalon, particularly in axons in the thalamus and the developing internal capsule, which is comprised of ascending thalamocortical and descending corticothalamic axons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: In IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, severe defects are observed in multiple forebrain axon tracts.
claims.source: In IspdL79*/L79* mutants, which lack glycosylated Dystroglycan, and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, in which Dystroglycan is deleted throughout the epiblast, we observed severe defects in multiple forebrain axon tracts (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 immunohistochemistry and DiI tracing shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Forebrain axon tract abnormalities in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants include fasciculated axons in the upper layers of the cortex.
claims.source: Abnormalities included fasciculated axons in the upper layers of the cortex (arrows), a large, swirling bundle of axons in the ventral telencephalon (asterisk), and a large axonal projection inappropriately exiting through the ventral diencephalon (arrowheads) (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: Observed in L1 immunostaining shown in Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: Forebrain axon tract abnormalities in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants include a large, swirling bundle of axons in the ventral telencephalon.
claims.source: Abnormalities included fasciculated axons in the upper layers of the cortex (arrows), a large, swirling bundle of axons in the ventral telencephalon (asterisk), and a large axonal projection inappropriately exiting through the ventral diencephalon (arrowheads) (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: Observed in L1 immunostaining shown in Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: Forebrain axon tract abnormalities in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants include a large axonal projection inappropriately exiting through the ventral diencephalon.
claims.source: Abnormalities included fasciculated axons in the upper layers of the cortex (arrows), a large, swirling bundle of axons in the ventral telencephalon (asterisk), and a large axonal projection inappropriately exiting through the ventral diencephalon (arrowheads) (Figure 2A–C).
claims.evidence: Observed in L1 immunostaining shown in Figure 2A-C.

claims.claim: The forebrain axon tract defects in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants are fully penetrant.
claims.source: These defects were somewhat variable in their severity, but were fully penetrant and all three of these defects were observed in all mutants.
claims.evidence: Observed across all mutant animals examined.

claims.claim: In IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, TCAs largely fail to cross the DTB and instead extend ventrally out of the diencephalon.
claims.source: In contrast, TCAs in both IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants largely failed to cross the DTB, and instead extended ventrally out of the diencephalon, often joining the optic tract (Figure 2E,F,K,L).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by DiI labeling of TCAs shown in Figure 2E, F, K, and L.

claims.claim: In IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, many CTAs fail to cross the PSPB.
claims.source: DiI labeling in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants indicated that many CTAs fail to cross the PSPB.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by DiI labeling of CTAs shown in Figure 2H and I.

claims.claim: CTAs that cross the PSPB in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants stall or take abnormal trajectories through the ventral telencephalon.
claims.source: Axons that do cross the PSPB stall or take abnormal trajectories through the ventral telencephalon (Figure 2H,I,K,L).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by DiI labeling of CTAs shown in Figure 2H, I, K, and L.

claims.claim: Few CTAs in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants correctly navigate through the internal capsule to arrive at the thalamus.
claims.source: Few CTAs in IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants were able to correctly navigate through the internal capsule to arrive at the thalamus.
claims.evidence: Observed from DiI labeling experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The anterior commissure is frequently diminished in IspdL79*/L79* mutants.
claims.source: The anterior commissure was frequently diminished in IspdL79*/L79* mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: Observed by L1 staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: In IspdL79*/L79* mutants, the lateral olfactory tract projects deeper into the ventrolateral forebrain instead of forming directly beneath the pial surface.
claims.source: In IspdL79*/L79* mutants, the LOT was consistently abnormal, often projecting deeper into the ventrolateral forebrain (arrowheads, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,F).
claims.evidence: Observed by L1 staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and F.

claims.claim: The corpus callosum in IspdL79*/L79* mutants appears largely normal.
claims.source: In contrast, the corpus callosum in IspdL79*/L79* mutants appears largely normal, despite the prominent number of axons projecting inappropriately into the upper layers of the cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,F).
claims.evidence: Observed by L1 staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and F.

claims.claim: Deletion of Dystroglycan throughout the neuroepithelium of the dorsal and ventral telencephalon in Dag1F/-;Foxg1Cre mutants results in abnormal projections in the internal capsule and abnormal axonal projections into the upper layers of the cortex.
claims.source: Using immunostaining and DiI labeling, we found that both TCAs and CTAs took abnormal trajectories in Dag1F/-;Foxg1Cre mutants that were similar to those observed in Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre and Ispd mutants (arrowheads, Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B').
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 staining and DiI labeling shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, B'.

claims.claim: The internal capsule is normal in Dag1F/-;Gbx2CreERT2 mutants.
claims.source: Based on L1 staining and DiI labeling of TCAs and CTAs, the internal capsule is normal Dag1F/-;Gbx2CreERT2 mutants (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,C').
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 staining and DiI labeling shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, C'.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is required in the telencephalon and not in TCAs during internal capsule formation.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that Dystroglycan is required in the telencephalon and not in TCAs during internal capsule formation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the normal internal capsule in Dag1F/-;Gbx2CreERT2 mutants (which delete in thalamus/TCAs) and abnormal internal capsule in Dag1F/-;Foxg1Cre mutants (which delete in telencephalon).

claims.claim: In Dag1F/-;Emx1Cre mutants, CTAs extend normally across the PSPB, through the internal capsule, and into the thalamus despite abnormal cortical lamination.
claims.source: Despite the abnormal cell body positioning of subcortically-projecting deep layer neurons, their ability to extend axons across the PSPB, through the internal capsule, and into the thalamus appeared unaffected (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 staining and DiI labeling shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is not required in CTAs during internal capsule formation.
claims.source: These results suggest that Dystroglycan is not required in CTAs during internal capsule formation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from normal CTA trajectories in Dag1F/-;Emx1Cre mutants where Dystroglycan is deleted from cortical neurons.

claims.claim: In Dag1F/-;Emx1Cre mutants, TCAs extend normally through the internal capsule but form fasciculated bundles that project into the upper levels of the cortex.
claims.source: Reciprocal projections from TCAs were likewise able to extend normally through the internal capsule in Dag1F/-;Emx1Cre mutants, but upon entering the cortex, formed fasciculated bundles that projected into the upper levels of the cortex (Figure 3D, arrows, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D').
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 staining and DiI labeling shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D'.

claims.claim: The abnormal TCA projection into upper cortical layers in Dag1F/-;Emx1Cre mutants is a secondary effect of migration defects in the cortex.
claims.source: We interpret this as a secondary effect of the migration defects in the cortex Dag1F/-;Emx1Cre mutants, as it resembles phenotypes seen when subplate neurons are mislocalized to the upper layers of the cortex (Molnár et al., 1998; Rakić et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison to phenotypes in cited literature.

claims.claim: CTAs and TCAs in Dag1F/-;Dlx5/6Cre mutants extend through the internal capsule and into their target regions normally.
claims.source: CTAs and TCAs in Dag1F/-;Dlx5/6Cre mutants extended through the internal capsule and into their target regions normally (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and E'), demonstrating that Dystroglycan is not required in guidepost cells in the internal capsule.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 staining and DiI labeling shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, E'.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is not required in guidepost cells in the internal capsule.
claims.source: CTAs and TCAs in Dag1F/-;Dlx5/6Cre mutants extended through the internal capsule and into their target regions normally (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and E'), demonstrating that Dystroglycan is not required in guidepost cells in the internal capsule.
claims.evidence: Inferred from normal axon guidance in Dag1F/-;Dlx5/6Cre mutants where Dystroglycan is deleted from LGE-derived guidepost cells.

claims.claim: The internal capsule, anterior commissure, lateral olfactory tract, and corpus callosum are all normal in Dag1βcyto/- mutants.
claims.source: L1 staining shows that the internal capsule, anterior commissure, lateral olfactory tract, and corpus callosum were all normal in Dag1βcyto/- mutants (Figure 3G, data not shown), demonstrating that intracellular signaling by Dystroglycan is completely dispensable for forebrain axon guidance.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by L1 staining shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Intracellular signaling by Dystroglycan is completely dispensable for forebrain axon guidance.
claims.source: L1 staining shows that the internal capsule, anterior commissure, lateral olfactory tract, and corpus callosum were all normal in Dag1βcyto/- mutants (Figure 3G, data not shown), demonstrating that intracellular signaling by Dystroglycan is completely dispensable for forebrain axon guidance.
claims.evidence: Inferred from normal forebrain axon tracts in Dag1βcyto/- mutants lacking the intracellular domain.

claims.claim: Dystroglycan is not required in CTAs, TCAs, or 'corridor' cells, but is required in neuroepithelial cells in the ventral telencephalon for forebrain axon guidance.
claims.source: Collectively, we conclude that Dystroglycan is not required in CTAs (Emx1Cre), TCAs (Gbx2Cre), or 'corridor' cells (Dlx5/6Cre), but is required in neuroepithelial cells in the ventral telencephalon (Foxg1Cre).
claims.evidence: Concluded from the pattern of phenotypes across different conditional knockout lines.

claims.claim: Celsr3 is a mammalian orthologue of the D. melanogaster planar cell polarity protein Flamingo.
claims.source: We therefore focused our attention on the transmembrane receptor Celsr3/Adgrc3, a mammalian orthologue of the D. melanogaster planar cell polarity protein (PCP) Flamingo.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Celsr3.

claims.claim: Celsr3 is a member of the adhesion GPCR family of proteins.
claims.source: Celsr3 is a member of the adhesion GPCR family of proteins, and its large extracellular domain contains two LG domains, identifying it as a potential Dystroglycan interacting protein (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Celsr3 structure.

claims.claim: The large extracellular domain of Celsr3 contains two LG domains.
claims.source: Celsr3 is a member of the adhesion GPCR family of proteins, and its large extracellular domain contains two LG domains, identifying it as a potential Dystroglycan interacting protein (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Shown in the schematic in Figure 4A and established knowledge about Celsr3 structure.

claims.claim: Celsr3 is highly expressed in commissural and motor axons in the spinal cord.
claims.source: Celsr3 is highly expressed in the developing nervous system, including commissural and motor axons in the spinal cord, and throughout the developing forebrain, including CTAs, TCAs, and Isl1 +guidepost cells in the ventral telencephalon (Chai et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2016; Onishi et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Established by previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Celsr3 is expressed throughout the developing forebrain, including CTAs, TCAs, and Isl1+ guidepost cells in the ventral telencephalon.
claims.source: Celsr3 is highly expressed in the developing nervous system, including commissural and motor axons in the spinal cord, and throughout the developing forebrain, including CTAs, TCAs, and Isl1 +guidepost cells in the ventral telencephalon (Chai et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2016; Onishi et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Established by previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Celsr3-/- mutants exhibit AP randomization of post-crossing commissural axons in the spinal cord.
claims.source: Celsr3-/- mutants also show remarkably similar axon guidance defects to IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, exhibiting AP randomization of post-crossing commissural axons in the spinal cord, as well as defects in anterior commissure and internal capsule formation in the forebrain (Onishi et al., 2013; Tissir et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Established by previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Celsr3-/- mutants exhibit defects in anterior commissure and internal capsule formation in the forebrain.
claims.source: Celsr3-/- mutants also show remarkably similar axon guidance defects to IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, exhibiting AP randomization of post-crossing commissural axons in the spinal cord, as well as defects in anterior commissure and internal capsule formation in the forebrain (Onishi et al., 2013; Tissir et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Established by previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Fc-tagged Dystroglycan binds specifically to AP-Celsr3-LG1 domain, but not the AP-Celsr3-LG2 domain.
claims.source: We found that Fc-tagged Dystroglycan bound specifically to Alkaline Phosphatase-tagged Celsr3-LG1 domain (AP-Celsr3-LG1), but surprisingly not the AP-Celsr3-LG2 domain (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: AP-Celsr3-LG1, but not AP-Celsr3-LG2, binds endogenous glycosylated Dystroglycan from brain lysate.
claims.source: Similarly, using tagged Celsr3-LG domains as bait, we found that AP-Celsr3-LG1, but not AP-Celsr3-LG2, was able to bind endogenous glycosylated Dystroglycan from brain lysate (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assay shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: AP-Celsr3-LG1 and AP-Slit-C-terminal domains bind to COS7 cells overexpressing Dystroglycan, whereas AP-Celsr3-LG2 does not.
claims.source: In a live cell binding assay, AP-Celsr3-LG1 and AP-Slit-C-terminal domains bound to COS7 cells overexpressing Dystroglycan, whereas AP-Celsr3-LG2 did not (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by live cell binding assay shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Celsr3-LG1 contains conserved basic residues, a Ca2+ binding site, and a glycine at the end of the loop that are present in other Dystroglycan-binding LG domains.
claims.source: Alignment of Celsr3-LG1 with Laminin-α2-LG4 shows significant sequence similarity, including the conservation of the basic residues, the Ca2+ binding site, and the glycine at the end of the loop (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Celsr3-LG2 lacks a Ca2+ binding site, the basic residues, and the glycine present in Dystroglycan-binding LG domains.
claims.source: In contrast to Celsr3-LG1, Celsr3-LG2 lacks a Ca2+ binding site, the basic residues, and the glycine, and exhibits no sequence conservation with other Dystroglycan-binding LG domains (data not shown), likely explaining its lack of binding.
claims.evidence: Stated based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Celsr3R1548Q-GFP shows similar subcellular localization and expression levels compared to wild-type Celsr3-GFP in 293 cells.
claims.source: Compared to wild-type Celsr3-GFP, in which the C-terminal 346 amino acids of the intracellular domain of Celsr3 were replaced with the coding sequence for EGFP, Celsr3R1548Q-GFP showed similar subcellular localization and both total and cell-surface expression in 293 cells, suggesting that the R1548Q mutation does not affect the folding or stability of Celsr3 (Figure 5B–C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunocytochemistry and western blotting shown in Figure 5B-C.

claims.claim: The R1548Q mutation does not affect the folding or stability of Celsr3.
claims.source: Compared to wild-type Celsr3-GFP, in which the C-terminal 346 amino acids of the intracellular domain of Celsr3 were replaced with the coding sequence for EGFP, Celsr3R1548Q-GFP showed similar subcellular localization and both total and cell-surface expression in 293 cells, suggesting that the R1548Q mutation does not affect the folding or stability of Celsr3 (Figure 5B–C).
claims.evidence: Inferred from normal expression and localization of Celsr3R1548Q-GFP.

claims.claim: AP-Celsr3-LG1R1548Q exhibits markedly reduced binding to DG-Fc compared to wild-type AP-Celsr3-LG1.
claims.source: Compared to wild-type AP-Celsr3-LG1, AP-Celsr3-LG1R1548Q exhibited markedly reduced binding to DG-Fc, indicating that the conserved binding interface is critical for the specificity of this interaction (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The conserved binding interface in Celsr3-LG1 is critical for the specificity of the Dystroglycan-Celsr3 interaction.
claims.source: Compared to wild-type AP-Celsr3-LG1, AP-Celsr3-LG1R1548Q exhibited markedly reduced binding to DG-Fc, indicating that the conserved binding interface is critical for the specificity of this interaction (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the loss of binding when the conserved residue is mutated.

claims.claim: AP-Celsr3-LG1 binds to post-crossing commissural axons in the ventrolateral funiculus of E12.5 spinal cord.
claims.source: In E12.5 spinal cord, AP-Celsr3-LG1 binding was observed in post-crossing commissural axons in the ventrolateral funiculus (arrows, Figure 5G), similar to the expression pattern of Dystroglycan (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by AP-section binding assay shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: AP-Celsr3-LG1 binds to axons in the internal capsule of E14.5 brain sections.
claims.source: In E14.5 brain sections, AP-LG1-Celsr3 binding was observed on axons in the internal capsule (arrows, Figure 5H), similar to the expression pattern of Dystroglycan (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by AP-section binding assay shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: AP-Celsr3-LG1R1548Q shows diminished binding in both the spinal cord and brain compared to wild-type AP-Celsr3-LG1.
claims.source: Furthermore, AP-Celsr3-LG1R1548Q showed diminished binding in both the spinal cord and brain (Figure 5I,J), consistent with our in vitro binding results (Figure 5D) and confirming the binding specificity between Dystroglycan and Celsr3-LG1.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by AP-section binding assay shown in Figure 5I and J.

claims.claim: Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice are viable and fertile.
claims.source: Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice are viable and fertile, as opposed to Celsr3-/- mice, which die immediately after birth due to respiratory defects (Tissir et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Observed from breeding and maintenance of Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice.

claims.claim: Celsr3-/- mice die immediately after birth due to respiratory defects.
claims.source: Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice are viable and fertile, as opposed to Celsr3-/- mice, which die immediately after birth due to respiratory defects (Tissir et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Established by previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Celsr3 protein in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice migrates at the correct molecular weight and is present at normal levels.
claims.source: Analysis of brain lysates indicated that Celsr3 protein in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice migrates at the correct molecular weight, is present at normal levels, and does not lead to compensatory changes in the levels of Celsr1 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by western blotting shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The Celsr3R1548Q mutation does not lead to compensatory changes in the levels of Celsr1.
claims.source: Analysis of brain lysates indicated that Celsr3 protein in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice migrates at the correct molecular weight, is present at normal levels, and does not lead to compensatory changes in the levels of Celsr1 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by western blotting shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In Celsr3WT/R1548Q heterozygous controls, 86.5 ± 2.52% of injection sites show normal anterior turning of commissural axons.
claims.source: In Celsr3WT/R1548Q heterozygous controls (B), DiI labeling of open book preparations shows that commissural axons extend through the floor plate, then execute an anterior turn in 86.5 ± 2.52% of injection sites (n = 7 animals, 49 total injection sites).
claims.evidence: Quantified from DiI labeling experiments shown in Figure 6B and 6D.

claims.claim: In Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants, only 22.32 ± 6.35% of injection sites show normal anterior turning of commissural axons.
claims.source: In contrast, only 22.32 ± 6.35% of injection sites in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants (n = 6 animals, 48 total injection sites) (C) show normal anterior turning, with the remaining 77.68% exhibiting AP randomization after crossing the floor plate, similar to Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre, IspdL79*/L79*, and Celsr3-/- mice.
claims.evidence: Quantified from DiI labeling experiments shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: 77.68% of injection sites in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants exhibit AP randomization after crossing the floor plate.
claims.source: In contrast, only 22.32 ± 6.35% of injection sites in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants (n = 6 animals, 48 total injection sites) (C) show normal anterior turning, with the remaining 77.68% exhibiting AP randomization after crossing the floor plate, similar to Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre, IspdL79*/L79*, and Celsr3-/- mice.
claims.evidence: Quantified from DiI labeling experiments shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: The AP randomization phenotype in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants is fully penetrant.
claims.source: This phenotype was fully penetrant, with all Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants showing abnormal turning at multiple injection sites.
claims.evidence: Observed across all Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants examined.

claims.claim: Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants do not exhibit floorplate stalling phenotypes.
claims.source: Importantly, none of the Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants exhibit the floorplate stalling phenotypes that are seen in IspdL79*, Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre, and Slit/Robo compound mutants, consistent with Celsr3's specific role in regulating anterior turning in post-crossing commissural axons.
claims.evidence: Observed from DiI labeling experiments and immunostaining.

claims.claim: Celsr3 has a specific role in regulating anterior turning in post-crossing commissural axons.
claims.source: Importantly, none of the Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants exhibit the floorplate stalling phenotypes that are seen in IspdL79*, Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre, and Slit/Robo compound mutants, consistent with Celsr3's specific role in regulating anterior turning in post-crossing commissural axons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the specific AP randomization phenotype without floor plate stalling in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants.

claims.claim: The overall structure of the ventrolateral funiculus in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants appears normal.
claims.source: E12.5 spinal cord sections labeled with antibodies to L1 or Robo1 and Robo2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E) confirm that the overall structure of the ventrolateral funiculus in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants appears normal.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-E.

claims.claim: Celsr3 interacts with Dystroglycan through its LG1 domain to direct the proper anterior turning of post-crossing commissural axons.

results.result: Dystroglycan functions non-cell autonomously as an extracellular scaffold during spinal commissural axon guidance and does not require signaling through its intracellular domain. Deletion of Dystroglycan from neuroepithelium (Sox2Cre) causes axon guidance defects, while deletion from axons themselves (Wnt1Cre) or removal of the intracellular domain (Dag1βcyto/-) does not affect guidance.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C21, C25-C26, C51-C52 provide converging genetic evidence from multiple conditional knockout lines showing that Dystroglycan is required in neuroepithelial cells but not in commissural axons themselves, and that the intracellular domain is dispensable. The open book preparations (C21) and immunostaining (C25-C26) provide quantitative and qualitative support. The experimental design appropriately tests cell autonomy using tissue-specific Cre lines.

results.result: Dystroglycan is required for proper formation of multiple forebrain axon tracts including the internal capsule, anterior commissure, and lateral olfactory tract. In IspdL79*/L79* and Dag1F/-;Sox2Cre mutants, severe and fully penetrant defects are observed including fasciculated axons in upper cortical layers, abnormal axon bundles in the ventral telencephalon, TCAs failing to cross the DTB, and CTAs failing to cross the PSPB.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C41 and C96 are well-supported by L1 immunostaining and DiI tract tracing experiments shown in Figure 2. The phenotypes are described as fully penetrant (C34) and observed across multiple mutant lines. The anatomical descriptions are detailed and supported by both immunohistochemistry and anterograde tracing. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=3-5 animals per genotype).

results.result: Dystroglycan is required in neuroepithelial cells of the ventral telencephalon, but not in thalamocortical axons (TCAs), corticothalamic axons (CTAs), or guidepost cells during forebrain axon tract development. Conditional deletion experiments using Foxg1Cre, Gbx2CreERT2, Emx1Cre, and Dlx5/6Cre demonstrate non-cell autonomous function.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C50, C53, and C118 are supported by systematic conditional knockout experiments using multiple Cre lines with different expression patterns. The logic is sound: Foxg1Cre (telencephalon) shows defects, while Gbx2CreERT2 (thalamus/TCAs), Emx1Cre (cortical neurons), and Dlx5/6Cre (guidepost cells) do not show internal capsule defects. The interpretation that C48 (TCA projection into upper cortical layers in Emx1Cre mutants) is secondary to migration defects is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Celsr3 binds to Dystroglycan through its LG1 domain but not its LG2 domain. The LG1 domain contains conserved residues (basic residues, Ca2+ binding site, glycine) found in other Dystroglycan-binding LG domains, while LG2 lacks these features.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C61-C65 are supported by multiple complementary binding assays (co-IP, pull-down from brain lysate, live cell binding) shown in Figure 4. The sequence alignment (C64) demonstrates conservation of key residues. The differential binding of LG1 vs LG2 is consistent across all assays. The structural rationale for LG2's lack of binding (C65) is logical based on sequence analysis.

results.result: The Dystroglycan-Celsr3 interaction through the LG1 domain is critical for anterior turning of post-crossing commissural axons in vivo. Celsr3R1548Q knock-in mice that cannot bind Dystroglycan show anterior-posterior randomization of commissural axons (77.68% of injection sites) similar to Dystroglycan mutants, but do not show floor plate stalling, indicating a specific role in anterior turning.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C66-C84 provide strong evidence through a well-designed knock-in experiment. The R1548Q mutation disrupts Dystroglycan binding in vitro (C68-C69, C72) without affecting protein stability or localization (C66-C67). The in vivo phenotype (C77-C80) closely matches the specificity predicted from the binding data. The absence of floor plate stalling (C81) distinguishes this from broader Dystroglycan loss-of-function phenotypes. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-7 animals). The quantification shows statistical significance (p<0.001, C77-C78).

results.result: The requirement for Dystroglycan:Celsr3 interactions is context-dependent. Forebrain axon tracts are normal in Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mutants despite abnormal spinal commissural axon guidance, indicating that Dystroglycan:Celsr3 interactions are not required in the forebrain.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C105-C106, and C111 are supported by L1 immunostaining and DiI labeling (Figure 6E-J) showing normal forebrain development in Celsr3R1548Q mutants. This contrasts with the spinal cord phenotype in the same animals, demonstrating context-dependence. The interpretation is logical and well-supported by the data.

results.result: The forebrain axon tract defects in Dystroglycan mutants likely reflect interactions with other LG-domain containing proteins such as Laminins or Slits rather than Celsr3. Slit/Robo mutants show similar forebrain phenotypes to Dystroglycan mutants, and Slits regulate both axon guidance and guidepost neuron migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C87, C113-C117, and C119 are largely speculative (C117, C119 explicitly marked as speculation). While the phenotypic similarity between Slit/Robo and Dystroglycan mutants (C113) is supported by citations, the direct involvement of Slit-Dystroglycan interactions in forebrain guidance is inferred rather than demonstrated. The normal forebrain in Celsr3R1548Q mutants (C85-C86) supports the conclusion that other partners must be involved, but the specific identity of these partners remains uncertain.

results.result: Celsr3R1548Q/R1548Q mice are viable and fertile with normal Celsr3 protein expression levels and localization, unlike Celsr3-/- mice which die at birth. The mutation does not cause compensatory changes in Celsr1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by western blotting data (Figure 6A) and breeding observations. The viability of Celsr3R1548Q mice contrasts with Celsr3-/- lethality (C74, supported by citation), demonstrating that the R1548Q mutation is hypomorphic rather than null. This is important for interpreting the specificity of the phenotype.

results.result: Dystroglycan functions as a multifunctional scaffold that coordinates extracellular matrix proteins, secreted cues, and transmembrane receptors to regulate axon guidance throughout the mammalian brain and spinal cord. Axon guidance defects are a key feature of dystroglycanopathy.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7, and C91 represent the overarching conclusions of the manuscript. They are well-supported by the combination of current findings (Celsr3 binding and function) and previous work (Laminin and Slit binding, cited in C7). The evidence spans multiple CNS regions (spinal cord and forebrain) and demonstrates interactions with different classes of molecules (ECM proteins, secreted factors, transmembrane receptors).

results.result: Background information on Dystroglycan and Celsr3 structure, function, and disease associations. Dystroglycan is a glycosylated transmembrane protein that binds LG-domain containing proteins and can signal through its intracellular domain. Celsr3 is an adhesion GPCR with two LG domains that is expressed in developing axons and shows similar axon guidance phenotypes to Dystroglycan mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 and C54-C60 are background information supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental results but do not represent new findings from this study.

results.result: Previous work from the authors showed that glycosylated Dystroglycan regulates axon guidance in the spinal cord and optic chiasm by maintaining the basement membrane and organizing Slit protein localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 accurately cite the authors' previous work. These findings provide important context for the current study and establish the foundation for investigating additional Dystroglycan binding partners.

results.result: Congenital mirror movements, which arise from improper decussation of corticospinal axons, have been reported in isolated cases of dystroglycanopathy, suggesting that axon tract abnormalities may contribute to the neuropathology of this disorder.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by citations to clinical literature. Claim C89 is established knowledge. However, claim C90 is explicitly speculative and the connection between the clinical observations and the experimental findings in this manuscript is indirect. The authors have not directly demonstrated corticospinal axon defects in their mouse models.

results.result: Proposed model: Celsr3 functions cell-autonomously in commissural axon growth cones and binds in trans to Dystroglycan in the neuroepithelium/basement membrane during floor plate crossing. This interaction is required for anterior turning in response to Wnt gradients involving Jnk and atypical PKC signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 represent a proposed mechanistic model. C92 is supported by citation (Onishi et al., 2013). C93 is a reasonable inference from the genetic and biochemical data presented. C94-C95 are supported by citations to previous literature. The model is consistent with all available data, though some aspects (particularly the molecular details of how Dystroglycan-Celsr3 binding regulates Wnt signaling) remain to be tested.

results.result: Background information on forebrain axon tract development and the roles of guidepost cells, Celsr3, and other guidance molecules. TCAs and CTAs navigate through the internal capsule using intermediate targets including Isl1+ guidepost neurons. Celsr3 is required in these guidepost neurons and in peripheral motor axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C103, C107, and C109 are background information supported by appropriate citations. Claim C104 summarizes phenotypic similarities between Dystroglycan and Celsr3 mutants based on data and citations. Claim C108 is speculation. Claim C110 reports negative data (no peripheral motor axon defects) that is mentioned but not shown. These claims provide context for interpreting the forebrain results.

results.result: Evolutionary conservation of Dystroglycan and Celsr3 function in axon guidance. Homologues in C. elegans (DGN-1, FMI-1) and D. melanogaster (Dg, Flamingo) show similar roles in axon guidance and targeting, suggesting evolutionarily conserved interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C127 are supported by citations to previous literature in model organisms. Claim C123 is speculation based on rescue experiments. Claim C128 is an inference about evolutionary conservation based on phenotypic similarities across species. The argument for conservation is reasonable but indirect, as direct molecular interactions have not been demonstrated in these other organisms.

results.result: Dystroglycan has multiple roles in nervous system development beyond axon guidance, including neuronal migration, synapse formation, glial development, and blood-brain barrier maintenance. During migration, Dystroglycan in neuroepithelial cells likely binds Laminins and Perlecan. At synapses, potential binding partners include Neurexins and other LG-domain proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C138 are supported by citations to previous literature. Claims C137, C139, C141, and C143 are speculative interpretations about binding partners and mechanisms. Claim C142 is clinical knowledge. These claims provide important context about Dystroglycan's broader functions but represent primarily literature review rather than new findings. The speculative claims (C137, C139, C141, C143) are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: Dystroglycan displays differential glycosylation patterns in different cell types (muscle, glia, neuronal subtypes) that correlate with binding capacity. This differential glycosylation likely has functional consequences in the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C144-C148 are supported by citations to previous literature. Claim C149 is speculation about functional consequences. The observation of differential glycosylation is well-established (C145-C147 cite Satz et al., 2010), and the correlation with binding capacity (C148) is established knowledge. However, the functional significance (C149) remains speculative.
